To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) wood‐grazing loricariid catfishes in Neotropical streams are specialized for different feeding modes and trophic niches, (2) wood‐grazers have robust jaws specialized for chewing wood and high δ15N values, and (3) surface grazers have long jaws and low δ15N values.

wood‐grazing Neotropical fishes partition their niche by exploiting different food resources associated with the surface and interior of coarse woody habitat, and that these fishes assimilate carbon from cellulosic wood and nitrogen from intermediate microbial decomposer sources in the environment.

the seven Neotropical loricariid fishes we studied partitioned coarse woody debris into three functional niches: (1) a group specialized for wood goung, (2) a group specialized to feed on the surfaces of wood, and (3) a group specialized as macroinvertebrate feeders that also forages on the surfaces of coarse wood.

the feeding biology of fishes, and particularly with how fishes partition their food resources.

wood-eating loricariid catfishes have specialized jaw morphologies and isotopic signatures that indicate assimilation of wood-derived C and N, while non-wood-eaters occupy different regions of jaw functional space and have isotopic signatures indicating assimilation of non-wood food resources.

we have demonstrated the importance of trophic specialization in the feeding ecology of wood-eating fishes, and that trophic specialization can be inferred from morphological and isotopically derived information.

the jaw functional morphologies of these seven loricariid catfish species are consistent with their respective feeding modes.
